clue.text: "Drink up" includes H-dropping Welsh boy and mob, our newish ...

definitions.note: the definition runs on into 2 down: our newish Oxford Companion to English Literature, i.e. its editor

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the drink word is read from bottom to top
the reversed drink word holds the boy's name inside it
dropping one's aitches means the letter H is left out of the boy's name

blocks.note: a dram is a small drink of spirits
a typical Welsh boy's name
a rabble is a disorderly crowd

explanation.surface: A party-goer downs a drink with a Welsh lad who drops his aitches, amid a rowdy crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 2 down: Margaret Drabble, the novelist, edited the 1985 edition of the Oxford Companion to English Literature, which was new when this puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist edited the fifth edition of that reference book, so she is the person behind the newish volume on English letters.

clue.text: ...  university fellow in Eng. Lit.

definitions.note: read with 1 down: the newish Oxford Companion to English Literature

blocks.note: the English university city
a fellow is a companion or comrade

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 down, it reads like a university fellow who teaches English literature.
explanation.walkthrough: Read together, 1 and 2 down say Margaret Drabble edited the Oxford Companion to English Literature; the ellipsis joins the two clues.
explanation.definitionFit: The full title of the reference book is the Oxford Companion to English Literature, so the book belongs in that field.

clue.text: Poor old story about fast ship

indicators.note: the old story goes around the word for fast, holding it inside

blocks.note: a tale is a story, especially a traditional one
Lent is the Christian season of fasting
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A dull yarn about a speedy vessel, judged poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like an adjective for the ship, but it is the period of fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without any gift or skill gives a poor performance, so the adjectives match in sense.

clue.text: Some common drug turned up by journalist is caused to disappear

indicators.note: only some of the drug's name is used, its first five letters
in a down clue, turned up means the letters run from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: the stimulant in coffee and tea, the commonest drug of all
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A reporter hides some everyday narcotic so that it vanishes.
explanation.definitionFit: To efface is to rub out or obliterate, so something effaced has been made to vanish.

clue.text: Soft music for 2

blocks.note: p is piano, the musical direction for soft
an air is a tune

explanation.surface: A gentle piece of music written for two players.
explanation.walkthrough: The 2 is not a cross-reference to 2 down here but just the number.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple of matching things make a set of two, so the noun stands for the number.

clue.text: Be calm - don't just play

blocks.note: first meaning: steady your nerves
second meaning: write your own music rather than perform others'

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense takes the phrase literally: a musician who composes the music personally is not merely playing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means settle down and regain control, while read word by word it urges writing music oneself.

clue.text: Verdict: semitonic change before finale

blocks.note: in music an accidental is a sharp or flat that shifts a note by a semitone
death is life's end

explanation.surface: A musical critic's judgment on a key change just before the closing movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical setting hides an inquest; an accidental is a sharp, flat or natural sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A coroner's inquest can return this finding when someone died through mishap rather than crime.

clue.text: Affix an upper-class arrangement with art that conceals art?

indicators.note: an arrangement puts the letters into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for upper-class

explanation.surface: Attach a posh flower arrangement made with skilful artlessness.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the Latin tag ars est celare artem: a studied simplicity is art hiding itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Faux-naif describes work that pretends to be innocent or untutored, a deliberate skill dressed up as simplicity.

clue.text: Make up for about a hundred without delay

indicators.note: the phrase for making amends goes around the letter for a hundred

blocks.note: to atone is to make amends
C is the Roman numeral for one hundred

explanation.surface: Compensate straight away for around a hundred wrongs.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means immediately, straight away, this very moment.

clue.text: Cut to a single point in blood

indicators.note: the point is placed inside the word for blood

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
gore is spilt blood
N is north, a compass point

explanation.surface: A wound sliced down to one spot amid the blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' suggests a wound, but it means snub someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut someone is to snub them deliberately, refusing to acknowledge their presence.

clue.text: Silver fibre for mats, they say - you can't write with it

indicators.note: they say signals that the fibre word is heard, not seen, so a different spelling is used

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
palm fibre used for matting; the palm genus is spelt with ph

explanation.surface: A metallic weave for mats that leaves you unable to write.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the medical term for loss of the ability to write, so a sufferer cannot put words on paper.

clue.text: Reminder not applicable to Catholics?

blocks.note: first meaning: a nudge to jog someone's memory
second meaning: Irish slang for a Protestant

explanation.walkthrough: In Northern Ireland a Prod is a Protestant, so the label cannot apply to a Catholic.
explanation.definitionFit: A poke or nudge serves as a reminder, and the slang name for Protestants excludes Catholics by definition.

clue.text: Old sins in Paris are very old hat

blocks.note: très is French for very
passés, French for out of date, plural to match are

explanation.surface: Ancient vices, a Parisian says, are terribly out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole wordplay is French: très passés means very old hat. 'Forgive us our trespasses' is the old wording of the Lord's Prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespasses is the archaic biblical word for sins or wrongdoings, as in the traditional Lord's Prayer.

clue.text: Lots of lawmen find heaven in a chattel

blocks.note: a posse is a band of men gathered by a sheriff
Sion, or Zion, the heavenly city

explanation.surface: Sheriffs' bands discover paradise in a piece of personal property.
explanation.walkthrough: Also the title of A. S. Byatt's Booker-winning novel, which 16 across refers to.
explanation.definitionFit: A chattel is an item of movable personal property, something one owns.

clue.text: Was 8 or 8, having hands laid on affectionately

blocks.note: first meaning: rowed in the stroke seat of an eight, which is numbered 8
second meaning: caressed gently

explanation.walkthrough: The 8s are not cross-references to 8 across: one is the eight-oared boat, the other the seat number of the oarsman who sets the rhythm.
explanation.definitionFit: The rower nearest the stern sits in seat 8 and sets the pace; separately, petting with the hand is a caress.

clue.text: 1's 22, one passed in the daytime, wrote 14

indicators.note: the word for passed sits inside the abbreviated day

blocks.note: a means one
Sat, short for Saturday, a day, then T for time
gone by means passed

explanation.surface: A sister of the novelist at 1 strolled past in daylight and wrote a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist A. S. Byatt is Margaret Drabble's elder sister, and her novel Possession won the 1990 Booker Prize.
explanation.definitionFit: Byatt is Drabble's sibling and the author of Possession, both facts pointing to the same novelist.

clue.text: Rub up perversely in silence

indicators.note: perversely means contrarily, so both rub and in are turned the wrong way round

blocks.note: rub turned round
in turned round
sh is a call for silence

explanation.surface: Polish something contrarily in a hushed room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rub' does double duty: it is part of the definition and, written backwards, the start of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To burnish metal is to polish it by friction until it shines.

clue.text: Crinkly fabric covers American copper left in the dusk

indicators.note: the fabric word covers and so wraps around the following letters

blocks.note: crêpe is a fabric with a crinkled surface
US is short for American
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
L is short for left

explanation.surface: Crinkled cloth wraps an American policeman abandoned at nightfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the metal's symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Crepuscule is a literary word for twilight, from Latin crepusculum.

clue.text: Funny girl's involved with us yet - could be Cinderella's

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd, so the letters come out strangely arranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The heroine of Funny Girl is mixed up with us yet, perhaps as a pantomime character.
explanation.walkthrough: Funny Girl is a musical, a distraction from the anagram signal. In the pantomime, Cinderella's two stepsisters are the Ugly Sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fairy tale and British pantomime, Cinderella has two unkind stepsiblings known by this name.

clue.text: A crooner to be a fellow 2?

definitions.note: a fellow of Oxford, i.e. a neighbouring Oxfordshire town

blocks.note: taken as written
Bing Crosby, the famous crooner
a don is a university fellow

explanation.surface: A crooning singer wants to become a university fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: The town sits just south of Oxford, so it is cheekily called a companion of the city in 2 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thames town lies a few miles from the university city, a near neighbour and companion to it.

clue.text: Where people sit (after standing) to eat

blocks.note: first meaning: a legislative assembly whose members stood for election
second meaning: what one eats, or to eat restrictedly

explanation.walkthrough: Standing here means standing for election; the Japanese parliament is a famous assembly of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a national assembly in some countries and also the food one habitually eats or restricts.

clue.text: See 19
A matter of the heart without the head, which is in recess

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the heart word goes around the head

blocks.note: taken as written
love is the heart's business
C is short for cape, a headland

explanation.surface: A romance gone headless, tucked away out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without the head' reads like beheading, but without here means outside, and the head is a cape.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcove is a recess set back into the wall of a room.

clue.text: Satirist finds girl in burrow

indicators.note: the girl is placed inside the animal's home

blocks.note: a sett is a badger's burrow
Moll is a girl's name, and slang for a gangster's girl

explanation.surface: A mocking writer discovers a young woman hiding in an animal's hole.
explanation.walkthrough: Tobias Smollett was an 18th-century Scottish novelist known for satire.
explanation.definitionFit: Smollett wrote satirical novels such as Humphry Clinker and Roderick Random.
